name: The Stanford Review

summary.text: The Stanford Review is a conservative and libertarian student newspaper at Stanford University, founded in 1987 by Peter Thiel and Norman Book. Thiel, who founded the paper at the end of his sophomore year, was its first editor-in-chief through his junior and senior years. The paper's own history notes that an earlier Stanford Review ceased to exist in 1984 and that the current paper has no continuity with it. Later editors-in-chief included Ken Howery and David Sacks, who went on to co-found and run PayPal with Thiel. Fortune reports that a 1990s lawsuit by Stanford students, some of them Review writers, ultimately compelled the university to overturn its campus speech code.

facts.claim: The Stanford Review's own history page says a group of undergraduates founded the paper in 1987 to spark campus debate by presenting alternative viewpoints, and names Peter Thiel as its first editor-in-chief. Thiel's first editor's note described the goals as presenting alternative views on current issues in the Stanford community and creating a forum for rational debate.
facts.quote: presenting alternative views on a wide range of current issues in the Stanford community and creating a forum for rational debate

openQuestions: The peter-thiel file records (from The New Republic's summary of Max Chafkin's biography) that the Review was started with grants from the Intercollegiate Studies Institute; no grant amounts or primary record were found and this was not re-verified.
The Ken Howery and David Sacks editorships are recorded in their own files; they were not duplicated here.
The speech-code lawsuit (Corry v. Stanford, 1995) was not opened; the claim rests on Fortune's description.
